transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-11
Start time: 17:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (VeroHealth Platform Lead), Tom Reynolds (VeroHealth SRE), Maya Singh (VeroHealth ML Engineer)

Summary: Quick scoping for a POC benchmark run: customer will bring their client scripts/traffic trace, Redwood will validate harness integration and propose streaming vs non-streaming run plan, success criteria to be codified (latency SLOs, throughput, cost target). Discussed fallback routing, KV cache behavior, and acceptance gating.

Topics: workload sizing, success criteria (p95/p99 targets), streaming fallback rules, harness adapter quirks, demons/edge-cases for client scripts, timeline and next steps.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Lena (Redwood): Alright welcome everyone, thanks for carving time. Quick intros, I'm Lena the AE, Diego's our SE. VeroHealth team, want to do short intros?
[00:18] Aisha (VeroHealth): Hi all, Aisha here, I own platform. We'll be running a clinical-assist feature behind our patient triage flow. Tom and Maya are on for SRE and ML.
[00:28] Tom (VeroHealth): Hi, Tom, SRE, I care mostly about tail latency and predictable cost.
[00:35] Diego (Redwood): Great. Today goal: agree on POC harness plan—what harness adapter we'll use for your client scripts, how we reproduce traffic (trace vs synthetic), and define acceptance criteria: throughput, p95/p99, cost per token ballpark.
[00:52] Maya (VeroHealth): Our current infra is a mix of server-side streaming calls and fallback non-streaming for async jobs. So we need both covered.
[01:03] Lena: Perfect, that's exactly what we wanted to hear. Two parallel things: 1) integration: get your scripts onto Redwood harness (we have an adapter pattern) and 2) benchmark config: streaming runs (simulate client chunked reads) vs non-streaming batch runs.
[01:22] Aisha: Small ask — we can't send PHI. We'll sanitize traces and we may obfuscate example prompts. Is that ok?
[01:30] Lena: Totally fine. We can run everything on obfuscated traces, or you can run the harness in your VPC private deployment if you prefer.
[01:39] Tom: We prefer hosted for speed of iteration but with data not leaving our tenancy; private control plane could be overkill. We'll evaluate.
[01:48] Diego: Noted. For the initial run we usually do hosted but with your obfuscated traces. We'll send an example harness config so you can validate locally. Link to repo: https://redwood.example.com/harness/VERO (sample).
[02:05] Maya: Great. A couple specifics from our side: target steady-state throughput ~350 qps for short bursts to 600 qps; average prompt lengths around 180 tokens; typical reply size 120 tokens. We also have long context flows (up to 2k tokens) sometimes.
[02:25] Diego: Good details. For sizing we'll plan a mix: 75% short prompts, 20% medium, 5% long. That distribution maps to GPU memory + KV cache behavior, so we can recommend quantized endpoints for baseline cost.
[02:42] Lena: Can we pin down acceptance thresholds? What counts as POC success vs optional?
[02:49] Aisha: Success is: 95th percentile latency under 350ms for streaming interactions, p95 under 600ms for non-streaming; p99 < 1.2s both modes; error rate < 0.5%; and a unit-cost target to be under our current provider by at least 15%.
[03:10] Tom: Also need cold-start worst-case tail < 2.5s, and we want KV cache behavior documented — particularly how prefix caching interacts with streaming chunking.
[03:21] Diego: We'll capture that. Note: streaming p95 is tricky because client-side chunking affects perceived latency. We'll instrument both server token-emit time and client first-byte time.
[03:34] Maya: That's important. For some flows users expect first token under 150ms.
[03:40] Diego: We'll surface both metrics: server-first-token and client-confirmed-first-chunk (harness simulates chunk assembly).
[03:48] Lena: On the harness adapter — quick primer: our harness takes a traffic trace or script and can replay in two modes: streaming-emulation and request-level. For streaming-emulation we emulate TCP chunking and backpressure, which matters for your frontend interaction. For request-level we do strict request/response timing for throughput.
[04:09] Aisha: How stable is the streaming emulation? Our client scripts do some weird things — they open multiple streams per session, cancel mid-response.
[04:18] Diego: We see that. We have a 'cancel' scenario in the harness where the script issues a cancel after N tokens. We can parameterize cancel rate. We also saw mis-transcripts where 'cancel' looked like 'cansel' but the harness handles that at the transport level, not NLP.
[04:32] Tom: Any known gotchas when integrating customer-side Python scripts? We have a custom client that uses asyncio and a connection pool.
[04:40] Diego: The adapter has two integration points: a lightweight shim you drop into your client runtime (python/ts) and a replay-mode where you point to a saved trace and the harness will replay. For asyncio you'll want to use the shim so we honor backpressure properly. We'll share snippet.
[04:56] Maya: Will the shim require code changes? We want to avoid heavy refactors.
[05:00] Diego: Minimal — a thin wrapper around send/receive. Example: replace raw call with harness.send(...) — we provide a compat-layer.
[05:08] Lena: Regarding resource targets, do you have any cost budget or constraint on GPU types?
[05:14] Aisha: We prefer to evaluate on A100-equivalent for parity with our current provider, but we'll also look at Ampere L7-style cheaper nodes if latency stays in range.
[05:25] Diego: For initial POC we'll provision dedicated capacity with an A100-ish profile to get clean comparatives. Then we can test quantized MPT-style model variants on cheaper nodes.
[05:34] Tom: Can Redwood do a hybrid run where we test streaming on hosted and non-streaming on a dedicated pool to compare?
[05:41] Diego: Yes, but note that routing differences can change cache hit-rates. We'll call that out in the analysis.
[05:49] Maya: What telemetry will you collect? We need per-token cost, model selection, kernel-type, batch sizes, and KV cache hit rate.
[05:58] Diego: We'll collect: token counts, server-first-token time, full-response time, batch size distributions, GPU utilization, and a KV cache metric. Some kernel names can be obfuscated in the hosted logs but we'll give the important mapping.
[06:13] Lena: Also we'll provide a benchmark report template: throughput vs latency curves, cost per 1k tokens, and sensitivity plots for different batch windows.
[06:22] Aisha: About timelines — can we get an initial harness run within two weeks?
[06:26] Lena: Yes, if you can send the 30-minute representative trace and sample scripts by 2026-05-18 we can run a first pass by 2026-05-22 and review the results with you.
[06:36] Tom: Works for us. Aisha will coordinate.
[06:40] Aisha: One more: our compliance folks want to see audit logs and SSO integration options — this will affect whether we run hosted or Private.
[06:48] Lena: We can surface audit logging detail. For POC run we provide log export with obfuscated keys, and SSO/SAML is part of Private onboarding later.
[06:57] Maya: On the streaming vs non-streaming decision — what are typical tradeoffs you see?
[07:02] Diego: Streaming usually reduces time-to-first-byte and improves perceived latency but can increase cost per session because of session overhead and smaller batch utilization. Non-streaming (batch) maximizes throughput/cost but may hurt perceived latency for interactive flows. Our recommendation: run both, measure first-byte p95 and end-to-end p95, then decide routing policy.
[07:22] Lena: For fallbacks, we typically implement a policy: prefer streaming model variant, if emitted tokens stall beyond threshold or GPU schedule is overloaded, fallback to a higher-throughput non-streaming variant or a smaller model. We can test that in the harness by injecting load spikes and verifying graceful degradation.
[07:40] Tom: Important: the fallback must preserve semantic fidelity — can't degrade to a model that produce unsafe/overconfident outputs for clinical text.
[07:48] Diego: Agreed. We'll only test fallbacks to model variants that have passed your safety checks. For the POC we can use a canned fallback that returns a predefined safe template if variant is incompatible.
[07:59] Maya: How do you measure semantic drift between models in the harness?
[08:03] Diego: We run a small eval set of prompts and compute embedding similarity and token-level differences; we also measure a handful of safety/regression checks as pass/fail. If similarity drops below threshold we flag. We'll include that in the final report.
[08:18] Aisha: Are there any client-side changes required for fallback? Like transparent retry vs user-facing error?
[08:24] Lena: Best practice is transparent server-side fallback where the client sees same API contract; the harness can emulate both strategies so you can choose.
[08:31] Tom: On acceptance criteria, let's capture specific numbers: streaming p95 <350ms, streaming p99 <1200ms, non-streaming p95 <600ms, overall error rate <0.5%, and cost per 1k tokens less than $0.85 (example).
[08:49] Lena: Noted, we'll codify those into the runner config as pass/fail gates.
[08:55] Maya: Anything we should watch for in our scripts? We have some subtle tokenization mismatches across model families.
[09:01] Diego: The harness normalizes tokenization by running the same tokenizer used in model side; however the client may pre-tokenize in rare cases. We'll flag tokenization diffs and propose fixes.
[09:11] Aisha: Can you also include a heatmap of long-tail requests and a breakdown of prompt templates that cause highest latency?
[09:18] Diego: Yes, the benchmark report will include a prompt-level breakdown and a small "actionable" section highlighting top 10 latency contributors.
[09:27] Lena: Next up operational questions: who will run the harness? Redwood can run the full run and share logs, or we can hand you the harness so you run it in your environment. Which do you prefer?
[09:38] Aisha: For speed, Redwood-first-run is fine. We'll run a repeat inside our VPC once we like results.
[09:44] Diego: Ok we'll run initial hosted run with obfuscated traces. We'll also stage a private run if you want to evaluate audit logs.
[09:52] Tom: How will you simulate long connections and connection churn? Our traffic has many short-lived sessions and occasional long polling.
[09:58] Diego: Harness parameters include session length distribution, inter-arrival time, and a churn factor. We'll use a Pareto distribution for session length unless you specify otherwise.
[10:08] Maya: On the topic of KB/Prefix caching — we have an edge cache for repeated patient contexts. How will the harness handle prefix cache warm-up?
[10:16] Diego: We can run warm-up phases in the harness where you replay hot prefixes at low concurrency to populate K/V cache. Then measure hit-rate during steady-state run. We'll annotate the report with cache hit curves.
[10:29] Aisha: Great. Also, small note: our legal requested that cost breakdown be per-route and per-token, not aggregated.
[10:36] Lena: We'll include per-route metrics; the console supports token-level attribution.
[10:42] Tom: For rollout strategy post-POC, we are thinking canary 5% traffic then 25% then 100% if SLOs hold. Can Redwood integrate with our traffic router?
[10:51] Diego: Yes, we have traffic-steering APIs and can provide canary configs. We can also run the harness to emulate canary ramp and show metric deltas.
[11:00] Lena: Alright let's summarize next steps and owners.
[11:03] Lena (summary): Redwood — share harness repo README and shim snippets (Diego), provision initial dedicated pool for comparative run, run hosted obfuscated-trace baseline. VeroHealth — provide 30-minute representative trace, list of critical prompts, indicate compliance constraints.
[11:18] Aisha: We'll aim to have trace and prompts by 2026-05-18.
[11:22] Lena: We'll target the baseline run by 2026-05-22 and follow-up review the week after.
[11:28] Tom: Please include safety checks and fallback policy in the report.
[11:31] Diego: Will do.
[11:33] Maya: Quick question — do you have examples of configured fallback thresholds?
[11:37] Diego: Yes, example policy: if first-token latency > 800ms OR server queue > 90% for > 10s then reroute to fallback; we'll share a policy template.
[11:46] Lena: Anything else?
[11:48] Aisha: No, that's it. Thanks.
[11:51] Lena: Thanks everyone. We'll send the artifacts after the call.

End of transcript.
